caveats: **Linux rows have three fields, not four.** The Linux leg emits `svc|name|status|description`; Windows and macOS emit four. A consumer that indexes by the schema's column names misreads Linux `status` and `description` as `display_name` and `status`, and has no startup type to read at all.

**A Windows enumeration failure looks like zero services.** If `OpenSCManagerW` or `EnumServicesStatusExW` fails, `enumerate_services_win` returns an empty list and the plugin sets no result status, unlike Linux and macOS, which forward a typed status for the same class of failure. Treat an empty Windows `list` on a host that should have services as unreliable, not as proof.

**macOS `status` is an exit code, and some labels never appear.** `status` is launchctl's last-exit code (`0` for nearly every row), so use the PID in the second field to tell whether a job is running. The list is capped at 512 rows with the `__truncated__` sentinel, and a launchd label containing a character outside letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `@` and `-` is dropped silently, without a status and without counting toward the sentinel's total.

**The macOS startup type is rarely known.** The join uses the `system` domain's override list only, so any label with no recorded override reads `unknown`; every row in the captured sample is `unknown`. That capture ran as an unprivileged user against the user's job list, so it does not show what the root daemon sees.

**`set_start_mode` has never been captured past validation.** Every OS sample stops at `error|missing required parameter: name`, so the `sudo`-wrapped and Win32 changes are verified from source and unit tests only. The Linux `list` and `running` captures also failed with `spawn_error`, so the three-field Linux row shape is likewise verified from source, not from a captured row.

definitions.description: Lists all installed system services regardless of their current state. On Windows, uses the Service Control Manager to enumerate Win32 services with name, display name, status, and startup type. On Linux, queries systemctl for all service units. On macOS, uses launchctl to list launchd services.

Lists only services that are currently running. On Windows, filters to SERVICE_ACTIVE state. On Linux, filters systemctl to --state=running. On macOS, filters launchctl output to services with a non-dash PID.

Changes a service's startup type to automatic, manual, or disabled. On Windows, uses the Service Control Manager (ChangeServiceConfig). On Linux, maps to systemctl enable/disable/mask. On macOS, uses launchctl enable/disable on the system domain. This is a state-changing action that requires role-gated approval.

description: System services — enumerate, query, and configure service startup types
how_it_works:
`list` and `running` read the host's service registry and return one `svc|` row per service: the Service Control Manager on Windows (Win32 services only, not kernel drivers), `systemctl list-units` on Linux (`--type=service` units that systemd has loaded, which is not every unit file on disk and excludes timers, sockets and other unit types) and `launchctl list` on macOS. `running` is the same read narrowed to services that are up: Windows asks the Service Control Manager for every state except stopped, Linux keeps systemd's `running` sub-state, and macOS keeps rows that have a PID (`launchctl` has no filter of its own, so the plugin filters after parsing). On macOS one extra call, `launchctl print-disabled system`, supplies each row's startup type; a label that domain holds no override for reads `unknown`.

`set_start_mode` is the only mutation. It checks the service name and mode, then changes one service's boot-time start setting and nothing else: it does not start, stop or restart the service. Windows sets the Service Control Manager start type. Linux runs `systemctl enable` for `automatic`, `unmask` then `disable` for `manual`, and `mask` for `disabled`. macOS runs `launchctl enable` or `disable` against `system/<label>` and refuses `manual`, because launchd only has enabled and disabled. Linux and macOS commands run as shell-free argv under a 20 second deadline, prefixed with `sudo -n --` unless the agent is already root. The plugin is deliberately not a change history; the TAR service collector does that separately.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Which services exist? | `list` | Every Win32 service the Service Control Manager knows, running or not | Every launchd job `launchctl list` reports, up to 512 rows | Every `.service` unit systemd has loaded (`--type=service --all`); a unit file that was never loaded does not appear |
| Is a service up right now? | `running` or `list` | `status` is the SCM state; `running` returns every service that is not stopped | The PID column is the answer (`-` means not running); `status` is a last-exit code, not a state | `status` is systemd's sub-state (`running`, `dead`, `exited`, `failed`) |
| Will it start at boot? | `list` (`startup_type`) | `automatic`, `boot`, `manual`, `disabled`, `system` or `unknown`; delayed-start reads as `automatic` | `automatic` (explicit enable override), `disabled`, or `unknown` (no override recorded, which is the common case) | Not answered: Linux rows have no startup field |
| Change how it starts | `set_start_mode` | Exact: automatic, manual or disabled | `automatic` or `disabled` only | `disabled` is a systemd mask, stronger than the other platforms' disabled |

What it cannot tell you: whether a service is healthy, why it stopped, what depends on it, or what changed since last time. An empty Windows result is not proof of zero services (caveat 2), and a Linux or macOS result with a non-OK status is a partial answer, not a clean one.

Safe workflow for `set_start_mode`:

1. Run `list` and record the service's current `startup_type` (Windows and macOS only; Linux gives no startup type to record).
2. Run `set_start_mode` with the target `name` and `mode`. The change takes effect at the next boot or login; a running service keeps running.
3. Run `list` again and confirm the new `startup_type` (Windows and macOS). On Linux this plugin has no read-back, so confirm with `systemctl is-enabled` by other means.
4. To undo, call `set_start_mode` with the value recorded in step 1. Windows `boot` and `system` start types cannot be restored, because the action only accepts `automatic`, `manual` and `disabled`.

Target restrictions: `name` is 1 to 256 characters from letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `@` and `-`, so a Windows service name containing a space, or a systemd instance name with escaped characters, cannot be targeted. The action needs the `endpoint-admin` role and passes the `AdminOrApproval` gate.

### Diagrams

The plugin validates input first, then makes exactly one start-setting change per call (Linux `manual` adds a best-effort `unmask` beforehand). Nothing starts or stops the service, and a failure produces a single `error|` line instead of the three success lines.

This shows why the two families of legs fail differently: Windows has no way to say it could not read, while Linux and macOS attach a typed status to any degraded run, so a status other than the default means the rows are incomplete.

inputs.description: The service identifier. On Windows, the short service name (e.g. "Spooler"). On Linux, the systemd unit name (e.g. "nginx.service"). On macOS, the launchd label (e.g. "com.apple.metadata.mds").
inputs.name: name

inputs.description: Target startup type. "automatic" starts the service at boot. "manual" prevents auto-start but allows on-demand start. "disabled" prevents the service from starting entirely (Linux: systemctl mask; macOS: launchctl disable).
inputs.name: mode

name: services

columns.description: The service's short identifier: a Win32 service name, a systemd unit name, or a launchd label. Values: free text.
columns.name: name

columns.description: Column 2, whose meaning is OS-specific. On Windows it is the Service Control Manager's human-readable display name. On macOS it holds the launchd job's numeric PID as a string, or "-" when not running (the platform has no per-service display name in `launchctl list`). It is NOT emitted on Linux at all -- the Linux leg's row carries only 3 pipe fields (name, status, description), so this column is absent from the wire, not merely empty. Values: free text (windows) · integer PID or "-" (darwin) · field absent (linux).
columns.name: display_name

columns.description: Column 3, whose meaning is OS-specific. On Windows it is the service's current SCM state. On Linux it is systemd's SUB state from `systemctl list-units`. On macOS it is launchctl's raw last-exit-status code for the job -- an integer as a string, NOT a running/stopped word; use the display_name (PID) column to tell whether a macOS service is currently running. Values: stopped, start_pending, stop_pending, running, continue_pending, pause_pending, paused, unknown (windows) · free text systemd SUB state, e.g. running, dead, exited, failed (linux) · integer exit-status code as a string (darwin).
columns.name: status

columns.description: Column 4: the service's configured startup type. On Windows this is the SCM's 5-state taxonomy. On macOS it is an honest 3-value read derived from a bulk `launchctl print-disabled` join -- a label with no explicit override reports "unknown" rather than a guessed default. It is NOT emitted on Linux at all (no 4th column on the wire), because the systemctl leg does not derive a startup type. Values: automatic, boot, manual, disabled, system, unknown (windows) · automatic, disabled, unknown (darwin) · field absent (linux).
columns.name: startup_type

columns.name: name

On macOS it holds the launchd job's numeric PID as a string, or "-" when not running (the platform has no per-service display name in `launchctl list`). It is NOT emitted on Linux at all -- the Linux leg's row carries only 3 pipe fields (name, status, description), so this column is absent from the wire, not merely empty. Values: free text (windows) · integer PID or "-" (darwin) · field absent (linux).
columns.name: display_name

columns.description: Column 3, whose meaning is OS-specific. On Windows it is the service's current SCM state (always "running" for this action's filtered result). On Linux it is systemd's SUB state from `systemctl list-units --state=running`. On macOS it is launchctl's raw last-exit-status code for the job -- an integer as a string, NOT a running/stopped word; this action's own running-filter is applied on the PID column, not this one. Values: running (windows, this action always filters to it) · free text systemd SUB state (linux) · integer exit-status code as a string (darwin).
columns.name: status

columns.description: Column 4: the service's configured startup type. On Windows this is the SCM's 5-state taxonomy. On macOS it is an honest 3-value read derived from a bulk `launchctl print-disabled` join -- a label with no explicit override reports "unknown" rather than a guessed default. It is NOT emitted on Linux at all (no 4th column on the wire), because the systemctl leg does not derive a startup type. Values: automatic, boot, manual, disabled, system, unknown (windows) · automatic, disabled, unknown (darwin) · field absent (linux).
columns.name: startup_type

columns.description: Literal "ok" on a successful mode change. On any failure the plugin instead writes a single "error|<message>" line and this row does not appear at all. Values: ok (the only value ever emitted).
columns.name: status

columns.description: The `name` parameter echoed back unmodified, on a successful mode change only. Values: free text — echoes the name parameter.
columns.name: service

columns.description: The `mode` parameter echoed back unmodified, on a successful mode change only. Values: automatic, disabled (all OS) · manual additionally on windows/linux (darwin rejects it before this row is ever written).
columns.name: mode

outputs_note: Rows are pipe-delimited, prefixed `svc|`, one per service. The row **shape** differs by OS, not just the values: Windows and macOS emit the four fields the schema names (`name|display_name|status|startup_type`, where macOS puts the PID in the second slot), but Linux emits only **three** (`name|status|description`), because that leg never derives a startup type. A consumer must branch on OS before indexing a row (the server's own device-page parser does). `set_start_mode` never writes a `svc|` row: on success it writes three lines, `status|ok`, `service|<name>`, `mode|<mode>`; on any failure it writes one `error|<message>` line and none of the three, with return code 1. There is no placeholder-row convention for the reads. On Windows an enumeration failure returns zero rows with no status; on Linux and macOS a degraded run sets a typed `UNAVAILABLE` or `CONSTRAINED` status before whatever rows were parsed and returns code 1. On macOS the row cap (512) ends the list with a `svc|__truncated__|-|<total>|-` sentinel row.

privileges.grant: `list`/`running`: none beyond the default account. `set_start_mode`: the plugin asks the Service Control Manager for `SC_MANAGER_CONNECT` and the target service for `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG`, so the right is decided by that service's access-control list. The plugin enables or checks no privilege itself; the `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` entry in `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` is not exercised by this code.
privileges.if_refused: `list`/`running`: a failed `OpenSCManagerW` or `EnumServicesStatusExW` returns an **empty** list with no error and no result status, so a refusal reads like "zero services". A single service whose configuration cannot be opened reports `startup_type` `unknown`. `set_start_mode`: failures are explicit `error|...` rows (`access denied changing service '<name>'`, `service '<name>' not found`, or the Win32 error code).
privileges.measured: 2026-09-07, bare-metal, captured as `SYSTEM`; `list` and `running` only, `set_start_mode` stopped at parameter validation

privileges.grant: None as root: the `sudo -n --` prefix is skipped when the agent's effective uid is 0. A non-root agent needs the sudoers grants `/bin/launchctl enable system/*` and `/bin/launchctl disable system/*` (the installed grant also covers `bootstrap`/`bootout`, which this plugin does not use).
privileges.if_refused: `list`/`running`: a failed `launchctl list` or `launchctl print-disabled` sets a typed `UNAVAILABLE` or `CONSTRAINED` status through the shared runner seam. `set_start_mode`: a `sudo -n` denial is captured (stderr merged into the output) and appended to the `error|launchctl command failed for '<name>' (exit=<n>)` line.
privileges.measured: 2026-09-07, bare-metal, captured as an unprivileged interactive user, not the root identity the daemon runs under
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root (the shipped LaunchDaemon has no `UserName` key)

privileges.grant: `list`/`running`: none. `set_start_mode`: the sudoers grant `systemctl enable`, `disable`, `mask` and `unmask` (`/bin/systemctl` and `/usr/bin/systemctl`); the `sudo -n --` prefix is skipped when the agent is root. Under the packaged unit's `NoNewPrivileges=true`, `sudo` cannot escalate, so this grant takes effect only on a unit without that setting.
privileges.if_refused: `list`/`running`: a typed `UNAVAILABLE` or `CONSTRAINED` status; the captured sample shows `subprocess_runner:spawn_error` on both because `systemctl` could not be resolved in the capture container, not because of a permission denial. `set_start_mode`: a missing grant surfaces as `error|systemctl command failed for '<name>' (exit=1): sudo: a password is required`.
privileges.measured: 2026-09-06, container, captured as root (`euid 0`), not the deployed unprivileged identity
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account by design (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`)

result_status.when: Every Windows read (including a failed one), every Linux/macOS read that completed cleanly, a successful `set_start_mode` on any OS, and every `set_start_mode` validation or platform-decision error (missing `name`/`mode`, unsafe name, invalid mode, macOS `manual`, a command that ran and exited non-zero). The plugin sets no status on these paths.
Linux/macOS `list`/`running`/`set_start_mode`: `systemctl`/`launchctl` (or `sudo`) could not be started or was not found; shown in `docs/samples/linux.txt`
The 20 second runner deadline elapsed and the child was killed
The `systemctl`/`launchctl` run was cancelled before it finished
The child was killed by a signal rather than exiting cleanly
Defined by the shared runner for a capped line count. This plugin sets no line limit, so it does not occur here.
Linux/macOS `list`/`running`: the captured output hit the runner's byte cap but the tool itself exited cleanly

macOS `list`/`running`: `launchctl list` exited cleanly but its output has no lines or no `PID\tStatus\tLabel` header. No `svc|` rows are emitted, so a failed read is distinguishable from a host with nothing running. Reported only when no runner failure has already set a status.

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result only.** Rows travel the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response into the ResponseStore (`response_retention_days`, default 90), queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`; the dashboard's generic result viewer renders `services` through its key/value fallback schema (`result_parsing.hpp`).

**Device pages "Get live info".** The `services` live-snapshot kind (`device.live.services` audit verb) dispatches `list` directly and re-parses the same 3-versus-4-field row shape to render the device card (`device_routes.cpp`, `device_ui.cpp`).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync inventory, TAR, or DEX and metrics: nothing here runs on a schedule; the plugin executes only when dispatched.

**Sensitivity.** `name`/`display_name` rows name installed services and applications on the host. Windows service display names, macOS launchd labels and Linux unit names are an installed-software inventory by another route. `status`/`startup_type` carry nothing beyond that service's own state. Nothing in any row identifies a specific device or person.

**Siblings:** `agents/plugins/tar/src/tar_service_collector.cpp` performs its own, independently implemented service enumeration (the same three OS mechanisms) for TAR's diff-based change detection; it shares no code with this plugin.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary), then `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data), then `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("crossplatform.service.list")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`; live snapshot via the device page's `services` kind.
